newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks regain most of Monday's lost ground.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks regain most of Monday's lost ground.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks powered higher on Tuesday as the bull market resumed after being derailed on Monday by the Japanese prime minister's comment on his country's U.S treasury holdings.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 153.80 points, or 2.02 percent, at 7,758.06 after Monday's 192-point drop, which was the second-steepest fall ever for the blue-chip index. The Dow is now back within near distance of last Friday's record close of 7,796.51.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 18.11 points, or 1.26 percent, to its 17th record high of the year at 1,452.43, propelled by gains in technology stocks.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,787 to 962 on active volume of 542 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Stocks rallied quickly as Japan moved overnight to calm Wall Street's fears that Japan might sell some of its huge U.S. Treasury holdings.

On Monday, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, responding to a question after a speech in New York, said that Japan had been tempted in the past to sell its holdings of U.S. Treasury securities and boost its gold reserves, but had not done so.
Japan came to the market's rescue overnight, and reassured financial markets that the country was not planning an imminent sale of its U.S. government bond holdings.
"The (Japanese prime minister's) comments seemed off-the-cuff. When people really took a look at them, they decided to get back in," said Kenneth Ducey, director of trading at BT Brokerage.
The market's comeback surprised many traders, particularly the strength of a late day rally which drove the Dow, already up 50 points, climbing more than 100 points in the last 90 minutes of trading.
"The market seems to be able to weather any bad news. It shakes it off, and goes back on its merry way," said Ducey.
Goldman Sachs chief market strategist Abby Joseph Cohen said that with the Dow at such lofty levels, such market swings are not as big as they seem on a percent basis.
"We're suffering from an optical illusion," she said during an investment conference in New York.
Still, at least one trader voiced some concern about the overwhelming bullishness and volatility.

"I think the market has put on a really good show here today ... but I do think we are moving toward the top end of a trading range and the market is overbought," said James Volk, director of equity trading at Jensen Securities.

Drug stocks, which helped lead the market lower Monday, snapped back strongly after Merrill Lynch upgraded Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. The stock jumped 8-3/8 to 84-3/4 and touched a 52-week high of 85-3/4.

Other drug stocks also set new year highs, including Pfizer Inc., up 4-3/8 to 115-5/8, Eli Lilly & Co. up 3-15/16 to 109-15/16, Merck & Co., up 4-1/2 to 103-1/8 and Warner-Lambert Co., up 3-3/8 to 118-3/4.

Airline stocks were left out of the rally after another Wall Street firm, Dillon Read, backed off previously bullish second-quarter profit estimates and downgraded some airlines. AMR Corp. lost 1-5/16 to 92-1/6, Continental Airlines Inc. slipped 5/8 to 34-1/4, Delta Air Lines Inc. fell 7/8 to 57-7/8 and UAL Corp. lost 7/8 to 72-7/8.

Among other individual issues, PacifiCare Health Systems Inc. tumbled more than 20 percent after the managed health care provider said its second-quarter earnings would fall below Wall Street expectations. The Class B shares fell 18-3/4 to 66-3/4.

Virginia bank Central Fidelity Banks Inc. rallied on news that it would be bought for $2.3 billion by Southeast regional bank Wachovia Corp. Central Fidelity jumped 5-15/16 to 37-13/16. Wachovia slipped 11/16 to 61-15/16.

Geotek Communications Inc. climbed 1-7/16 to 6-5/16 on expectations its expanded pact with IBM will bolster the wireless communication company's revenues. It was the most heavily traded stock on Nasdaq.
Qwest Communications Inc. surged 27 percent in its market debut, closing up 6 at 28. The company is building a nationwide fiber-optic network that piggybacks on existing railroads.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 17.72 to 896.34. The American Stock Exchange index slipped 0.56 to 619.86.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 7.68 to 466.17. The average share was up 73 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 8,460.857, up 130.868, or 1.57 percent.
